name: Ammonite
luster: Dull, pearly or metallic depending on mineralisation
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of stability
Crystal healers link it to a sense of slow steady renewal
Many people keep it nearby for calm
summary: Ammonite is a spiral fossil from extinct sea creatures over 65 million years old, used in crystal tradition for patience, grounding and growth.
intro: An ammonite is the spiral-shelled fossil of an extinct marine animal related to squid and octopus, which swam in prehistoric seas from about 400 to 66 million years ago. Its shell grew in a perfect coil, divided into chambers, and after death was buried in sediment, where minerals gradually replaced the original material. Some are rough and brown, others glitter with golden pyrite or glow with the rainbow iridescence of ammolite. Sizes range from thumbnail to larger than a dinner plate. Slice an ammonite and you will see crystal-lined chambers, and polished halves are especially popular. It is a fossil that invites you to trace its curve with a finger.
history: People have found and treasured ammonites for thousands of years. The Greeks and Romans noticed their resemblance to the curved horns of the god Ammon, giving the name ammonite, and Pliny recorded the name. In India, ammonites known as shaligram stones are sacred to Vaishnavites as manifestations of Vishnu. In medieval England, ammonites were thought to be coiled snakes turned to stone, and Whitby carvers added snake heads to them, selling them as relics of Saint Hilda, according to legend. Fossils from Lyme Regis inspired early palaeontology, and Mary Anning collected here. Today, ammonites are used as a geological time marker and as decorative stones.
meaning: The spiral is a primal symbol of growth, cycles and the movement from the centre outward, and ammonite is the stone of this pattern. Practitioners say it carries the energy of deep time, encouraging patience, perspective and trust in slow, steady progress. It is linked to the Root and Earth Star for grounding, and to the Solar Plexus for personal confidence. Many people use it when starting a long project or while recovering a sense of balance. Because it is a fossil, it is also a symbol of survival and the preservation of something precious through enormous change. Some combine it with meditation on the golden ratio, tracing the spiral with their eyes. These ideas are traditional associations, not medical claims.
howToUse: Hold an ammonite in your palm and trace its spiral slowly with your finger as a calming focus. Keep one on your desk as a reminder to build step by step. Place a half-polished ammonite on a shelf in the living room, or in the northeast or southwest of the home for stable energy. Use a small fossil as a worry stone. In a grid, put it at the centre as a spiral focus for intentions. Carry a tiny pyritised ammonite in a pocket for confidence during long projects.
care: Ammonites are sturdy but can be brittle, especially pyritised or fractured specimens. A quick rinse is usually fine for calcite-filled pieces, but dry them well, and avoid soaking pyritised ones, which can rust or crumble over time. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or a selenite plate. Sunlight is safe. Store in a padded box, as fragile edges can chip. Dust with a soft brush and avoid harsh cleaners that remove natural patina.
identify: Real ammonites show a coiled shell with ribbing, chamber lines called sutures and sometimes crystal-filled cavities. They are heavy, being stone replaced shell. Beware of resin or plaster casts, which feel light, show no suture detail or have a uniform surface. Some Moroccan ammonites are enhanced, glued or partly carved. Madagascan pieces are often polished to reveal colour. Ask whether a specimen is complete or composited, and note that very large, perfect pieces are often restored.

faq.a: It is the fossilised shell of an extinct sea creature related to squid and octopus. They lived from about 400 to 66 million years ago, and their coiled shells became fossils preserved in rock.
The spiral stands for growth, cycles and patience. In crystal tradition, ammonite supports grounding, perspective and trust in slow, steady progress, and is kept by people starting long projects.

Brief rinsing is usually fine, but avoid soaking, especially for pyrite-replaced specimens, which can degrade. Dry thoroughly after any contact with water, and use smoke, sound or moonlight for cleansing instead.
